title: Chickweed salve for dry, itchy skin
subtitle: A cooling salve for dry skin, mild eczema, and heat rash
excerpt: Dried chickweed infused into olive oil, then set with beeswax at a 1:4 ratio. Traditionally applied to dry, itchy skin, mild eczema, and heat rash for longer-term skin management. Makes approximately 100 g of salve, which keeps for 12 months.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), Chickweed (Stellaria media) entry : emollient and cooling skin applications. Traditional western herbal preparation ratios: infused oil 1:5 herb to oil by weight; salve 1:4 beeswax to oil by weight.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Salve keeps for 12 months in a sealed tin in a cool dark place. Prepare in a single session using the double-boiler oil method.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in a sealed tin in a cool dark place. Discard if the surface develops white spots or the salve smells rancid.

glossaryTerms.definition: A preparation that softens and soothes the skin by forming a protective layer that reduces water loss.

content.text: Chickweed salve is a mild, cooling skin preparation made in two stages: dried Stellaria media leaf is first gently infused into olive oil at 60-65°C for 2-4 hours, then combined with beeswax at a 1:4 ratio to set into a firm salve. Traditionally used as an
emollient
for dry, itchy skin, mild eczema, and heat rash for ongoing skin management. The finished salve keeps for 12 months in a sealed tin.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Chickweed has no significant safety flags for external use at these preparation levels. Patch-test on a small area of skin before first use.

See the red flags section below for skin conditions that need medical attention rather than a home remedy.

Paediatric use: external application is generally well tolerated in children. Consult a paediatric doctor or herbalist for use on infants under six months.

content.text: Ingredients
Method
Stage 1: Make the infused oil
Place 20 g of dried chickweed and 100 ml of olive oil into the top vessel of a double boiler. Stir to combine.

Heat over a low flame. Use a probe thermometer to hold the oil at 60-65°C. Maintain this temperature for 2-4 hours, checking every 30 minutes. Do not let the oil overheat; above 70°C the herb's cooling active compounds begin to degrade.
Remove from the heat and cool for 10 minutes. Strain through muslin cloth into a measuring jug, squeezing the cloth well. You should have approximately 80-90 ml of pale green-tinted oil.
Stage 2: Make the salve
Return the strained infused oil to the clean double boiler. Add 25 g of beeswax pellets.
Warm gently, stirring, until the beeswax has fully melted. Drop a small amount onto a cold saucer to check the set. Firm up with more beeswax if too soft; loosen with a little more oil if too hard.
Pour into clean salve tins or small jars. Leave undisturbed for 30 minutes to set before lidding.
Dosing

Apply a thin layer to the affected skin once or twice a day. For ongoing dry or itchy skin, use for up to four weeks at a time. For heat rash or acute itch, apply up to three times a day until resolved.
Storage

Store in a sealed tin or jar in a cool dark place. The salve keeps for 12 months. Discard if the surface develops white spots or the smell turns rancid. Use a clean spatula rather than fingers to avoid contaminating the tin.
When not to use this remedy
See a GP for eczema that is weeping, crusted, infected (gold-coloured crust), spreading rapidly, or interfering with sleep. Eczema in infants warrants GP review rather than home remedies.
See a doctor for skin irritation that spreads, weeps, blisters, or comes with fever, and for any rash in someone unwell, which needs urgent assessment.
